newsitem.title: GERMANY: Finland hopes Germany to be cornerstone of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Finland hopes Germany to be cornerstone of EMU.

text.p: Finland's Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on Wednesday said he hoped Germany would recover from its economic difficulties to lead the European Union into the launch of its planned single currency.

Lipponen, who met Chancellor Helmut Kohl here at the start of a two-day visit, said the German leader was determined to meet both the timetable and the convergence criteria set by the Maastricht Treaty governing economic and monetary union (EMU).
Kohl, Lipponen told reporters, was fully aware that failure to meet those goals "would lead to disruptions in the markets and an appreciation of the mark".

Despite calls from some economists and central bankers for a delay in EMU to give Bonn time to get the economy and state finances into better shape, Lipponen said there were "grounds for optimism" that Germany can fulfil the Maastricht criteria.

Germany has insisted that the treaty's budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product be strictly adhered to, but many independent analysts say a weak economy will stop Finance Minister Theo Waigel hitting that target.

More bad news emerged on Wednesday when several German federal states said tax revenues in the first three months of this year were sharply below forecast -- with Kohl's home state of Rhineland Palatinate as much as 11 percent short.

Lipponen said Germany's significance was emphasised by the tasks of modernising EU institutions, the single currency and plans for eastward enlargement. To put those developments on a firm foundation, it was important the German economy picks up.
"It is important for all of Europe that the German economy does better," Lipponen told a news conference.
Lipponen said Finland was the only country apart from Luxembourg to meet all the Maastricht criteria and it should join EMU from the start.

But he acknowledged that, with one faction in his five-party ruling coalition calling for a "time-out" before deciding to join the currency union, Finland would have to adopt a wait-and-see position before making a final commitment.
"Of course, we can only take a final decision when we can see how the monetary union will look," he said.
